papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Multilingual Safety and Assessment of Large Language Models
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety of large language models (LLMs) across different languages and contexts. It introduces multilingual safety benchmarks, assesses safety in Chinese LLMs, and provides a comprehensive survey of safety threats and defenses for large models. The findings indicate that LLMs tend to produce more unsafe responses in non-English queries and highlight the necessity for tailored safety measures in various languages and applications.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily emphasize safety assessment but may not fully address the underlying biases in training data or the cultural nuances that affect safety perceptions. Additionally, while benchmarks are proposed, their effectiveness in real-world applications remains to be validated. The focus on specific languages may limit generalizability to other linguistic contexts.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies critical gaps in the safety of LLMs, particularly in non-English contexts, and underscores the need for comprehensive safety frameworks that accommodate multilingual and multicultural considerations. It supports research on enhancing safety measures and understanding the implications of deploying LLMs in diverse settings.

summary: Recent literature emphasizes the importance of interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs) to improve safety and controllability. Studies suggest that enhancing transparency in how LLMs process and generate language can mitigate risks associated with unintended outputs. Techniques such as attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation are explored to provide insights into model decision-making, fostering trust and enabling better alignment with human values.
scholarly_positioning: While recent studies have highlighted the significance of interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs), existing approaches often fall short in providing comprehensive insights into model behavior, particularly in high-stakes applications. Techniques like attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation, while useful, do not fully address the complexities of model decision-making, leaving gaps in understanding the nuances of safety and controllability. This proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing novel interpretability frameworks that not only enhance transparency but also align LLM outputs more closely with human values, addressing unresolved tensions between model complexity and user trust. By situating this work within the broader discourse on AI safety, it seeks to contribute to a more robust understanding of how LLMs can be made safer and more controllable.

research_scope: This study will investigate the effectiveness of novel interpretability frameworks for large language models (LLMs) in the context of automated customer support systems. The target population will include users interacting with these systems, focusing on their trust and satisfaction levels. The evaluation period will span three months, during which different interpretability techniques will be applied, including attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation. A control group will utilize standard LLM outputs without enhanced interpretability features. Primary outcomes will include user trust calibration measures and satisfaction ratings, while secondary outcomes will assess the accuracy of model outputs and the frequency of unintended responses.
concept_definition:
{
  "Large Language Models (LLMs)": "Advanced AI models designed to understand and generate human language, such as GPT-3 or BERT.",
  "Internal Representations": "Hidden states or activations within the model that capture information about input data, which can be analyzed for interpretability.",
  "Interpretability": "The degree to which a human can understand the reasoning behind a model's predictions or outputs.",
  "Attention Visualization": "A method that highlights which parts of the input data the model focuses on when making predictions, aiding in understanding model behavior.",
  "Layer-wise Relevance Propagation": "An interpretability technique that assigns relevance scores to input features based on their contribution to the model's output.",
  "Probing": "A method used to analyze internal representations by training simpler models on specific tasks to infer what information is encoded in the LLM.",
  "Attribution": "Determining which input features most significantly influence the model's output, often used to explain predictions.",
  "Sparse Autoencoders": "Neural network architectures used to learn efficient representations of data by forcing sparsity in the hidden layers, aiding interpretability.",
  "Activation Steering": "A technique to manipulate internal activations to achieve desired outputs, enhancing controllability.",
  "Safety Monitor": "A system designed to detect and mitigate unsafe outputs from LLMs, ensuring safe interactions.",
  "Explanation Generation": "The process of creating understandable rationales for a model's decisions, aimed at users or stakeholders.",
  "User Trust": "The confidence users have in the system's reliability and accuracy, which can be measured through trust calibration, blind trust, perceived transparency, and appropriate reliance.",
  "Safety Outcomes": "Metrics that evaluate the safety of model outputs, including unsafe response rate, over-refusal, jailbreak success, harmful compliance, and refusal precision/recall.",
  "Trust Calibration": "The alignment between a user's perceived trust in the system and the actual performance of the system, influencing user satisfaction and reliance."
}
technical_feasibility: The study requires access to open-source LLMs or models with hidden-state extraction capabilities, as internal representations will be analyzed. It also necessitates labeled datasets for training and evaluation, human participants for trust calibration measures, and ethics approval for user interaction studies. Additionally, GPU resources will be essential for running the models and conducting the experiments. If only API models are available, the design should be revised to focus on output-level explanations or black-box evaluations instead of internal representations. A feasible adjustment would be to utilize a combination of open-source models for interpretability analysis and API models for user trust studies, ensuring a comprehensive evaluation of both aspects.
gap: Prior studies have demonstrated the importance of interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs) for enhancing safety and controllability in high-stakes applications; however, they treat the effectiveness of these interpretability techniques in real-world user interactions as secondary, leaving unclear whether user trust and satisfaction are significantly influenced by enhanced interpretability features. This matters practically because improving user trust can lead to better adoption and reliance on automated systems; therefore, this study investigates the impact of novel interpretability frameworks on user trust and satisfaction in automated customer support systems within the defined scope.
question: How do novel interpretability frameworks, such as attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation, impact user trust and satisfaction in automated customer support systems compared to standard LLM outputs without enhanced interpretability features?
theoretical_mechanism: The independent variable is the implementation of novel interpretability frameworks (e.g., attention visualization, layer-wise relevance propagation) in large language models (LLMs). The mediator for system-level outcomes, such as unsafe response rate and controllability, is the enhanced transparency provided by these frameworks, which improves the understanding of internal representations and model decision-making. User-level outcomes, including trust and satisfaction, are influenced by the perceived transparency of the model's outputs, which acts as a psychological mechanism mediating the relationship between interpretability and user experience. The theoretical framework is grounded in the interplay between technical mechanisms (e.g., safety detection and steering) and psychological mechanisms (e.g., calibrated trust). The causal chain posits that improved interpretability leads to better safety outcomes, which in turn enhances user trust and satisfaction. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the effectiveness of interpretability techniques in real-world interactions and the degree to which perceived transparency influences user trust and satisfaction.
hypothesis: The implementation of novel interpretability frameworks, such as attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation, in large language models will significantly increase user trust and satisfaction in automated customer support systems compared to standard LLM outputs without enhanced interpretability features, mediated by the perceived transparency of the model's decision-making process.

Potential confounding variables include user familiarity with AI systems, prior experiences with customer support, and individual differences in trust propensity.

The study can claim that enhanced interpretability frameworks improve user trust and satisfaction in automated systems. methodology: This study will employ a controlled between-subject design to evaluate the impact of novel interpretability frameworks, specifically attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation, on user trust and satisfaction in automated customer support systems. Participants will be randomly assigned to either the experimental group, which interacts with LLM outputs enhanced by interpretability techniques, or the control group, which uses standard LLM outputs without these features. The primary operationalized variables include perceived transparency, user trust, and user satisfaction, measured through surveys and trust calibration metrics post-interaction. Safety outcomes, such as the unsafe response rate, will be monitored during the intervention. Statistical analyses will include comparisons of means between groups and regression analyses to assess the mediation effect of perceived transparency. Confounding variables such as prior experience with AI systems will be controlled through participant screening. The methodology ensures reproducibility by utilizing open-source LLMs and standardized evaluation metrics, while the three-month evaluation period allows for a thorough assessment of user interactions.

proposal: This research proposal aims to investigate the impact of novel interpretability frameworks, specifically attention visualization and layer-wise relevance propagation, on user trust and satisfaction in automated customer support systems, addressing a critical gap in the literature regarding the effectiveness of these techniques in real-world interactions. While prior studies have established the importance of interpretability in large language models (LLMs), they often overlook user trust and satisfaction, particularly in high-stakes applications. This study will define key concepts such as Large Language Models (LLMs), internal representations, interpretability, and user trust, while assuming access to open-source models and ethical approval for participant interactions. Positioned within the discourse on AI safety, this work seeks to bridge the gap between technical mechanisms of model decision-making and user experience, positing that enhanced transparency through interpretability frameworks will improve both safety outcomes and user trust. The research question focuses on how these frameworks influence user perceptions compared to standard LLM outputs, with the theoretical mechanism suggesting that improved interpretability enhances perceived transparency (system-level outcome), which in turn increases user trust and satisfaction (user-level outcomes). The hypothesis is that implementing these frameworks will lead to significantly higher user trust and satisfaction, measured through trust calibration metrics and satisfaction ratings. The methodology will employ a controlled between-subject design with appropriate baseline comparisons, ensuring reproducibility and robust evaluation of safety outcomes, such as the unsafe response rate. Expected contributions include a theoretical framework linking interpretability to user trust, a comparative analysis of interpretability techniques, and empirical evidence on their influence in high-stakes AI applications. Key limitations include potential confounding variables related to prior user experience with AI systems, and a risk matrix outlines failure modes such as participant engagement issues and the effectiveness of interpretability techniques, with corresponding mitigation strategies to ensure the study's integrity.
